children.value: All rank means lie near the expected value and the rank standard deviations match the theoretical expectation closely, indicating well-calibrated posteriors without substantial systematic biases. Two points are worth noting. First,

shows a mild left-shift (rank mean 527), which is a benign boundary effect (47% of participants have cue_sensitivity above 0.9, and posteriors near the upper bound of 1.0 cannot spread above it, producing a small downward estimation bias (≈ −0.02 to −0.07) confined to the ceiling). It does not affect the cue-aware-versus-cue-blind distinction the parameter is used for. Second,
is cleanly calibrated (rank mean 478, no boundary contraction), and

, although weakly recovered as a point estimate (see below), is well calibrated (rank mean 509), so its posteriors are honest and its limited signal appears as appropriately wide credible intervals rather than as bias.

children.value: ), is weaker by design: its target behaviour (oddball attribution) is governed by few informative events per session, a third of which are diffuse or hedged responses rather than a clean stay-versus-follow decision (see
). The recovery error follows a regression-to-the-mean profile, and the addition of the action-level

parameter reduces nr recovery by approximately 0.17 (from ≈ 0.63 with placement_noise fixed to ≈ 0.46 with it free, in a matched RF screen) by veiling the action-level features that carry the nr signal. Consequently, the reduced nr recovery is a signal-dilution effect rather than a parameter confound, since the within-posterior correlation between nr and placement_noise is ≈ 0. Accordingly

is reported with its posterior uncertainty rather than as a precise point estimate. Its calibration is nonetheless sound (see the SBC results above): the weak point-recovery is not accompanied by miscalibration, so the posteriors are honest and the limited signal manifests as appropriately wide credible intervals.
